lines: You already use Claude Code. This is what happens when you stop driving every session yourself, and build a factory that does it: how it's organised, what it checks, and how it gets better.

AI coding has moved in three steps. First, an assistant on your laptop: you prompt, you check every edit. Then remote agents: you type a prompt in the Claude app on your phone, and it builds in a cloud sandbox. And in parallel, factories: not about where the agent runs, but how the work is organised.

Side by side. Local and remote agents differ mostly in where they run. A factory changes who decides, who checks, and what's recorded: requirements you approve before anything is built, a separate checker agent, evidence for every check, and two approvals instead of one.

Here's the definition I find most useful, from Dru Knox at Tessl. A software factory is any agentic system where all of the code you ship is written by agents. Your job changes: you stop building the product, and build the machine that builds it.

How do you measure a factory? Three numbers, in order. Autonomy: how often a person has to correct or nudge the agents. Automation: how much runs without anyone reviewing it. And quality. You earn automation by proving autonomy first.

What makes autonomy safe is verification. You can only stop reading every line if something else checks it, every time, and leaves a record you can inspect. Without that, a factory is just a faster way to ship mistakes.

And a factory runs in three loops. The inner loop: agents iterate before anything goes up for review, fast and cheap. The outer loop: the thorough checks that replace review time. And the meta loop: it reads the corrections and failures, and fixes the factory itself, so the same mistake doesn't happen twice.

Here's the factory I built, on Claude Code. Eleven stages. Scripts read the issue, lint the plan, re-check the evidence, run the tests, publish a preview, and open the merge request. Agents write the requirements, the plan, and the code. And a person approves twice.

The pipeline is just data. Each stage says who does it, an agent, a script or a human, which skill it follows, and what it may write. A stage can fail three times before the factory stops and asks a person.

And each kind of job has a skill: a short written instruction the agent follows. This one is for UI logic. Pure functions, no DOM, no clock. And notice the last line: the maker doesn't tick its own task or write its own evidence.
Let's watch one real request go through it.
It starts as an issue in GitLab, in plain words, with the factory label. A webhook starts a pass straight away.
Within a minute the requirements agent has written the request up, and the factory stops at the first gate.
Requirements are user stories with acceptance criteria. Everything downstream is checked against these, so this approval actually means something.
The reply is one word on the issue. No slash: GitLab swallows a comment that's only slash-approve.
Then the plan. The work is split into sections, each naming the skill to use, and each ending in a gate the checker must pass.

And these are the checker's gates, written in the plan before any code exists. Runnable commands with expected results: the module's exports, no DOM or network access, currency formatting, and totals exact to the cent.

This is the inner loop. A maker session builds a section. A separate checker session, which never saw the maker work, runs the gate. Pass, and the next section starts. Fail, and a fresh maker gets the written findings.
The checker writes its evidence: each check, expected, found, and a verdict. Four sections in this run, four passes, first time.
Then the outer loop: a script re-runs the evidence checks rather than trusting them, the full test suite runs, and a preview goes up.
The person who asked tries the real thing in a browser, and approves again.
And a merge request opens, with the specs and every evidence file linked. Merging stays with a human.

How it runs. A GitLab issue or comment fires a webhook. That starts a pipeline on a runner. Each pass restores the factory's state from a branch, runs flow dot py through the stages, launches claude dash p for each agent stage, pushes the work branch, comments on the issue, and saves its state again.

Mapped to the loops. Inner loop: maker and checker per section, three attempts. Outer loop: scripts and tests, then a person tries it. And the meta loop: every time a person has to step in, it's recorded on the issue, and the fix goes into a skill or the rules. Honestly, today that loop is me, by hand.
The numbers from that run. Seventeen minutes from issue to merge request, approvals included. Ten agent runs. About a dollar twenty at API prices. And every section passed its checker first time.

And the limits. Checks prove the checks pass, not that the spec was right, which is why a person approves it. The meta loop is still manual. The runner works one request at a time. And it's best on small, clear requests.
Want to try it? There's a playground: your own GitLab project, nothing to install. File an issue and watch it go through. The code is open source, and the longer read is on Medium.
